summary: This RFC creates an IANA registry called "Post-Stack First Nibble" for the first 4 bits immediately after an MPLS label stack. It also sets requirements for registering new values, so MPLS packet processing is easier and more robust.

eli5.summary: Right after the address labels, the first few bits tell what comes next. This makes an official list of what each value means so devices don't confuse them.

questions: mpls first nibble after label stack
how to identify mpls payload type
why deprecate heuristic mpls load balancing
what is a post-stack header in mpls
subtitle: A registry and standards for the first 4 bits following an MPLS label stack.

tldr.problem: MPLS equipment needs to identify what comes after the label stack (IP packet, Ethernet frame, or a special header), and used a heuristic by examining the first 4 bits. This heuristic fails dangerously for non-IP packets that happen to start with bits that look like an IP version number.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC creates an IANA "Post-Stack First Nibble" registry to formally document what each 4-bit value means. It also deprecates the heuristic method and recommends using explicit headers or entropy labels for load balancing instead.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now deterministically identify post-stack content without guessing, and MPLS packet handling is more robust. Equipment manufacturers have clear documentation of the 16 possible values.

today: RFC 9790 is a Standards Track document published in July 2025 that creates the IANA "Post-Stack First Nibble" registry. The heuristic method for identifying MPLS payloads is now deprecated in favor of explicit post-stack headers. New MPLS implementations and deployments should use entropy labels or dedicated labels for load balancing rather than attempting to parse payload types from the first nibble.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) packets have a structure of three parts: a Layer 2 header, a label stack (the routing instructions), and then a payload (the actual data being delivered). The payload can be an IPv4 packet, an IPv6 packet, an Ethernet frame, or many other types. Additionally, there may be a Post-Stack Header (PSH)—a special control structure placed between the label stack and the payload to convey information to intermediate routers.

The problem is that MPLS equipment cannot automatically know what comes after the label stack. MPLS packets lack a built-in "payload type" field. To handle packets correctly, routers examine the first nibble (the first 4 bits) of the data after the label stack and try to guess its meaning.
sections.eli5: MPLS packets are like envelopes with address labels on top of them. After you peel off the labels, you need to know what's inside: a letter, a photo, or something else. There are no markings, so routers guess by looking at the first four bits.

sections.title: The Heuristic Problem
sections.content:
Equipment has traditionally used a simple heuristic: if the first nibble is 0x4, the payload is an IPv4 packet (IPv4 headers start with version number 4); if it is 0x6, the payload is IPv6 (version number 6); otherwise, the payload is assumed to be non-IP and the router falls back to simpler handling.

This heuristic works well when MPLS carries plain IP packets. However, it fails when MPLS carries an Ethernet frame or other Layer 2 data that does not happen to be IP. An Ethernet frame's destination MAC address is 6 bytes (48 bits), and the first nibble of the organizationally unique identifier in that address can randomly be 0x4 or 0x6. When this happens, the router incorrectly treats the Ethernet frame as an IP packet and attempts to extract load-balancing fields from random offsets in the frame, producing unpredictable behavior.

Even worse, routers use this guessing for load balancing across multiple paths (ECMP). Misidentification causes traffic to be distributed unevenly, wasting network capacity. The RFC deprecates this heuristic approach and recommends explicit methods instead.
sections.eli5: The guessing trick works fine for IP packets but breaks for other kinds of packets. Sometimes an Ethernet frame starts with the same pattern as IPv4 or IPv6, and the router then looks for load-balancing info in the wrong place, splitting traffic badly.

sections.title: Defining a Registry
sections.content:
Instead of relying on heuristics, this RFC creates a formal IANA registry for the Post-Stack First Nibble (PFN). A registry allows all 16 possible 4-bit values to be documented and assigned to specific uses. Equipment can then look up what a value means based on the context established by the label stack itself.

The key insight is that the PFN's meaning is not determined by the value alone. The same nibble value can mean different things depending on which labels precede it. For example, a PFN of 0x0 could indicate a pseudowire control word, a DetNet control word, or a Network Service Header—each with different structures. Context from the label stack disambiguates them.
sections.eli5: Instead of guessing, routers now have a reference book: if you see a 0x0 here, it could mean this; a 0x1 means that. The routers also look at the labels to know which meaning applies.

sections.title: The Post-Stack First Nibble Registry
sections.content:
The registry defines all 16 possible nibble values. PFN 0x0 is assigned to post-stack headers like control words (pseudowire, DetNet) and Network Service Header. PFN 0x1 is for associated channel headers used in MPLS, DetNet, and pseudowires. PFN 0x2 is for NSH OAM. PFN 0x3 is currently unassigned.

PFN values 0x4 and 0x6 are reserved for backward compatibility: they remain the IPv4 and IPv6 version numbers. This preserves legacy behavior where a bare IP packet (no PSH) appears after the label stack. Values 0x5 is assigned to BIER headers. Values 0x7 through 0xF are currently unassigned and available for future use.

The registry uses "Standards Action" assignment policy, meaning new allocations require an RFC and IESG approval. This ensures careful consideration before each nibble value is committed to a specific use.
sections.eli5: The list assigns each of the 16 possible values to a purpose: some are for headers that routers parse, some are reserved for IP, one is for a special replication header, and others are for future use.

sections.title: Deprecating the Heuristic
sections.content:
This RFC updates RFC 4928, which had described heuristic load balancing. The old text suggested restricting first nibble values to 0x0 and 0x1 to avoid future confusion with new IP versions. The new text is more direct: for any non-IP MPLS payload, equipment MUST use a Post-Stack Header with a PFN value that is neither 0x4 nor 0x6.

This requirement ensures that non-IP payloads are always marked explicitly, so the heuristic cannot misidentify them. For load balancing, the RFC recommends using dedicated mechanisms such as Entropy Labels or Flow-Aware Transport labels, which explicitly carry hash material for multipath decisions. This eliminates the need to snoop at payloads.

The recommendation is that new implementations and deployments MUST NOT use the heuristic guessing method. Legacy routers may continue to use it, but new devices follow the explicit-header approach.
sections.eli5: The new rule says: if it is not an IP packet, put a header on it that says so. Do not rely on guessing. For splitting traffic across multiple paths, use special labels designed for that job instead of peeking at the payload.

sections.title: Load Balancing and Future IP Versions
sections.content:
A concern in earlier specs was that a future IP version 0 or IP version 1 might exist, and devices using the heuristic would fail to load-balance those packets correctly. The deprecation of the heuristic resolves this concern. Since new equipment will not rely on the PFN value to identify IP packets, future IP versions (if they ever arise) can use any nibble value without disrupting ECMP. The context-based approach via labels handles any future protocol version.

This represents a step toward more deterministic and robust MPLS data plane processing. The long-term goal is to completely eliminate non-PSH MPLS encapsulation of non-IP data, but that requires evidence that no widely deployed routers still depend on the heuristic.
sections.eli5: Because we are stopping the guessing, future versions of IP can use any number they want without breaking load balancing. We are making the system more reliable for the future.
